questions.q: What kind of food do you enjoy eating most?
questions.model: I'm really fond of home-cooked noodle soup, to be honest. It's light but full of flavour, and my mum's recipe is my absolute favourite. On weekends I usually make a big pot for the whole family, so it's become a comforting tradition that we all look forward to.

vocab.meaning: made in a home kitchen, not bought ready-made
vocab.example: Nothing beats a home-cooked meal after a long week.

vocab.meaning: making you feel relaxed and cared for
vocab.example: A bowl of hot soup is incredibly comforting on a cold evening.

vocab.meaning: a custom passed down in a family or culture
vocab.example: Cooking together on Sundays is a tradition in my family.

questions.q: Do you prefer eating at home or in restaurants?
questions.model: Most of the time I'd rather eat at home. It's far cheaper, and I can control exactly what goes into my food. That said, I do enjoy dining out occasionally, like last month when we celebrated my sister's graduation at a lovely little Italian place.

vocab.meaning: eating a meal in a restaurant
vocab.example: We go dining out only on special occasions.

vocab.meaning: sometimes but not often
vocab.example: I occasionally treat myself to a fancy dessert on Fridays.

vocab.meaning: marked a happy event with a special activity
vocab.example: They celebrated their anniversary with a candlelit dinner downtown.

questions.q: Has the food you eat changed since you were a child?
questions.model: Definitely. As a kid I lived on fried snacks and sugary drinks, but these days I try to eat a balanced diet with plenty of vegetables. I became more health-conscious after a friend of mine got ill, and honestly I feel much more energetic now.

vocab.meaning: eating a healthy mix of different foods
vocab.example: Doctors say a balanced diet keeps you strong and focused.

vocab.meaning: careful about staying healthy
vocab.example: My brother is very health-conscious and avoids processed food.

vocab.meaning: full of energy and ready to be active
vocab.example: I always feel more energetic when I sleep properly.

questions.q: Is there any food you really dislike?
questions.model: Yes, I can't stand very spicy dishes. The first time I tried a hot curry, my eyes were watering and I couldn't taste anything else. I know many people love that kick, but it's simply not for me, so I always ask for the mild version.

vocab.meaning: strongly dislike something
vocab.example: I can't stand the smell of boiled cabbage in the kitchen.

vocab.meaning: not strong or spicy in taste
vocab.example: She ordered a mild curry because she dislikes strong spices.

vocab.meaning: a sharp, strong taste, usually from spice
vocab.example: This sauce has a real kick that wakes you up.

questions.q: How often do you use public transport?
questions.model: Almost every day, actually. I take the bus to university because parking is a nightmare and fuel is expensive. The journey takes about forty minutes, but I use the time to catch up on podcasts, so it never feels like wasted time.

vocab.meaning: the act of travelling from one place to another
vocab.example: The journey to the airport took nearly two hours.

vocab.meaning: do something you haven't had time for
vocab.example: I use weekends to catch up on sleep and housework.

vocab.meaning: an extremely unpleasant experience
vocab.example: Driving downtown at rush hour is a nightmare.

questions.q: What are the advantages of public transport in your city?
questions.model: The biggest advantage is that it's affordable, so even students can get around easily. It also reduces traffic congestion, which is a huge problem here. For example, the new metro line cut my commute in half and made the air noticeably cleaner.

vocab.meaning: cheap enough for most people to pay
vocab.example: Public buses are an affordable option for low-income families.

vocab.meaning: too much traffic making movement slow
vocab.example: Congestion in the city centre worsens every morning.

vocab.meaning: the regular trip between home and work
vocab.example: My daily commute used to take over an hour.

questions.q: Would you like to see any changes to public transport where you live?
questions.model: Yes, I'd love to see more frequent services in the evenings. At the moment the last bus leaves around ten, which is a real hassle if you work late. I think extending the timetable would make the whole system far more reliable for commuters.

vocab.meaning: happening often
vocab.example: Frequent trains mean you never wait long on the platform.

vocab.meaning: something annoying that causes trouble
vocab.example: Changing buses three times is a real hassle.

vocab.meaning: able to be trusted to work well
vocab.example: A reliable bus service gets people to work on time.

questions.q: Do you enjoy reading in your free time?
questions.model: I do, although I'm not as avid a reader as I used to be. I mostly read novels before bed because it helps me unwind after a stressful day. Lately I've been working through a detective series, and I'm completely hooked on it.

vocab.meaning: very enthusiastic about a hobby
vocab.example: My grandfather is an avid reader of history books.

vocab.meaning: relax after working or feeling stressed
vocab.example: Listening to soft music helps me unwind in the evening.

vocab.meaning: so interested that you cannot stop
vocab.example: I got hooked on that show after watching one episode.

questions.q: Do you prefer reading paper books or e-books?
questions.model: I'm a paper-book person, really. I like the feel of turning real pages, and I find it easier to concentrate without notifications popping up. E-books are handy for travelling, though, so I usually carry one on my phone for long train rides.

vocab.meaning: give all your attention to one thing
vocab.example: It's hard to concentrate when the room is so noisy.

vocab.meaning: useful and convenient
vocab.example: A small torch is handy during a power cut.

vocab.meaning: alerts that appear on a phone or computer
vocab.example: I switch off notifications when I need to study.

questions.q: Did you read a lot when you were a child?
questions.model: Yes, quite a lot. My father used to read me bedtime stories, and later I borrowed picture books from the school library every week. Looking back, those habits sparked my imagination and probably helped me do well in language classes.

vocab.meaning: caused something to begin or grow
vocab.example: That documentary sparked my interest in marine biology.

vocab.meaning: the ability to picture new ideas in your mind
vocab.example: Children with a vivid imagination often love storytelling.

vocab.meaning: things you do regularly without thinking
vocab.example: Good study habits take months to build properly.

questions.q: What kind of things do you read online?
questions.model: Mostly news articles and the occasional blog about travel. I skim headlines over breakfast to stay up to date, then I save longer pieces for later. I'll admit I sometimes fall into a rabbit hole of random videos, which is a bit of a time sink.

vocab.meaning: read quickly to get the main idea
vocab.example: I usually skim the report before reading it properly.

vocab.meaning: keep informed about the latest news
vocab.example: She reads two newspapers to stay up to date.

vocab.meaning: an activity that wastes a lot of time
vocab.example: Social media can easily become a huge time sink.

cue.topic: Describe a time you helped someone
bullets: and explain how you felt afterwards

part2.model: I'd like to talk about the time I helped my neighbour, Mrs Lan, who is in her seventies and lives alone. It happened last winter when a severe storm knocked out the power across our whole street. I knew she would be struggling in the dark, so I grabbed a torch and went straight over to check on her. She was visibly shaken, and she couldn't find her medication because the hallway was pitch black. I helped her locate it, then I brought some blankets and heated soup on our gas stove. I ended up staying with her for about three hours until the electricity finally came back on. The reason she needed help was simple. Her family live abroad, and she doesn't really know how to use a smartphone, so she had no way of contacting anyone. Before leaving, I wrote my number on a card and stuck it beside her phone in case of emergencies. Afterwards I felt incredibly rewarding, to be honest. It wasn't a big gesture, but she was so grateful that she cried a little. That evening made me realise how a small act of kindness can strengthen the bond between neighbours, and we've been much closer ever since.

vocab.meaning: having great difficulty doing something
vocab.example: She was struggling to carry all the heavy shopping bags.

vocab.meaning: completely dark
vocab.example: The forest was pitch black once the sun went down.

vocab.meaning: feeling thankful for what someone did
vocab.example: I'm so grateful for your support during exams.

vocab.meaning: a close connection between people
vocab.example: Shared experiences build a strong bond between friends.

vocab.meaning: a caring action done to help others
vocab.example: A simple act of kindness can brighten a stranger's day.

structure: Introduce the person and the situation (who you helped and when)
Explain what the problem was and why they needed help
Describe step by step what you did to help
Explain the result and how you felt afterwards
Finish with what you learned or how things changed

roundingOff.q: Do you think most people are willing to help others in an emergency?
roundingOff.model: I'd say the majority are, yes. When something goes wrong, people tend to forget their differences and step in without thinking twice. I've seen strangers push a broken-down car off a busy road, and that kind of spontaneous teamwork always restores my faith in humanity.

vocab.meaning: get involved to help in a difficult situation
vocab.example: Teachers had to step in to stop the argument.

vocab.meaning: done naturally without planning
vocab.example: Their spontaneous applause surprised the nervous performer.

vocab.meaning: brings back a feeling or belief
vocab.example: Good news like this really restores my confidence in people.

questions.q: Why do some people choose to volunteer while others do not?
questions.model: I think it largely comes down to personality and available time. People who are naturally empathetic tend to feel a strong urge to give back, whereas those with demanding jobs often simply can't spare the hours. Another factor is upbringing, because children who see their parents volunteering usually follow the same example when they grow up. Personally, I believe schools and families should encourage generosity much earlier, so it becomes natural.

vocab.meaning: able to understand and share other people's feelings
vocab.example: An empathetic nurse listens carefully to every patient.

vocab.meaning: do something good in return for what you received
vocab.example: Many graduates want to give back to their old schools.

vocab.meaning: the way parents raise and teach a child
vocab.example: His strict upbringing taught him to respect every elder.

questions.q: How has technology changed the way people help each other?
questions.model: It has made helping far quicker and easier. Crowdfunding websites, for instance, allow thousands of strangers to raise money for a sick child within days. On the other hand, some argue that clicking a donate button is rather impersonal and may replace face-to-face support, which is arguably more meaningful for those in need. Personally, I think the best approach is to use both, so technology supports real human contact.

vocab.meaning: raising money online from a large number of people
vocab.example: Crowdfunding helped the village rebuild its flooded school.

vocab.meaning: lacking warmth or a personal touch
vocab.example: A generic email reply can feel rather impersonal.

vocab.meaning: possibly, according to a reasonable point of view
vocab.example: She is arguably the best speaker in our class.

questions.q: Should the government or individuals be responsible for helping people in need?
questions.model: Ideally it should be a shared responsibility. Governments have the resources to provide a safety net, such as healthcare and unemployment benefits, which charities simply cannot match. However, individuals fill the gaps by offering personal, flexible support. So I believe a combination of both works best for any healthy society. In my experience, countries that combine both approaches seem noticeably fairer and more stable overall.

vocab.meaning: a system that protects people when things go wrong
vocab.example: Unemployment benefits act as a safety net for workers.

vocab.meaning: money, staff or materials available for use
vocab.example: Small charities often lack the resources to expand quickly.

vocab.meaning: a mixture of two or more things together
vocab.example: A combination of exercise and diet improved his health.

questions.q: Do you think people in big cities are less willing to help strangers than those in small towns?
questions.model: There's some truth in that. In small towns everyone knows each other, so there's a strong sense of community and people look out for one another. City life is busier and more anonymous, which can make people hesitant to get involved. That said, I've seen plenty of generous city dwellers, so it's not a rule. In my own experience, a friendly greeting can quickly break the ice, whichever kind of place you live in.

vocab.meaning: with no one knowing who you are
vocab.example: Living in a huge city can feel lonely and anonymous.

vocab.meaning: unsure and slow to act
vocab.example: Shy students are often hesitant to ask questions in class.

vocab.meaning: a feeling of belonging to a close group
vocab.example: Local festivals create a strong sense of community here.

questions.q: What role can schools play in teaching young people to be community-minded?
questions.model: Schools can play a huge role. Organising regular volunteer projects, like cleaning up parks or visiting care homes, gives students first-hand experience of helping. Teachers can also encourage cooperation through group work. If children learn early that small contributions matter, they are much more likely to become responsible and caring adults. I have seen this work well in my old school, where pupils still volunteer long after graduating.

vocab.meaning: gained directly through your own experience
vocab.example: Interns get first-hand experience of working in a hospital.

vocab.meaning: working together towards a shared goal
vocab.example: Team success depends on honest cooperation between members.

vocab.meaning: things you give or do to help a group
vocab.example: Every student's contributions made the festival a success.

phrases: Schools can play a huge role

questions.q: Is it better to give money to charities or to give your time?
questions.model: Both are valuable, but I'd lean towards giving time. Money is useful, yet it can disappear into administration costs, whereas volunteering creates direct, visible change. Spending a weekend teaching kids to read, for example, can transform a life in a way a small donation rarely does, and it builds lasting relationships. Ideally, people should do a bit of both depending on their circumstances and what is most needed.

vocab.meaning: slightly prefer one option over another
vocab.example: I lean towards the second plan because it's cheaper.

vocab.meaning: change something completely, usually for the better
vocab.example: A good teacher can transform a child's confidence.

vocab.meaning: money or goods given to help a cause
vocab.example: Her generous donation paid for new library books.
